This one is above your threshold, 5 files. Want to predict while it works? Say skip to pass.

Two questions, then I will leave you alone until it is done. I will not tell you whether you are right yet.
Fine. My guess: AdminOrders.jsx, api/admin.js, server/routes/admin.js, server/controllers/adminController.js, and server/db/orders.js for the query to fetch all rows.

That's a solid set across the full path, client page, api layer, route, controller, and db query. Given the conventions here, what would each of those five actually do, in your own words, starting with the button in AdminOrders.jsx?

AdminOrders.jsx adds a download button that calls the api function and triggers a file save; admin.js adds a request to a new export endpoint expecting a CSV blob; routes/admin.js wires that endpoint to a controller method; adminController.js fetches all orders via the db layer and converts rows to CSV text with proper headers; db/orders.js just needs a query to pull the full orders table unfiltered for that export.

Got it, recorded. Now set the files aside for a moment: walk me through what happens in order, starting the instant the user clicks that button, through to the CSV landing on their machine. What is step one, step two, and so on?
Agent needs you. I will wait.
Back. Nothing else from me until it is done.

Click fires the download handler, which calls the api function hitting GET /admin/orders/export; server controller queries all orders from db/orders.js, builds a CSV string with headers, sets Content-Type text/csv and Content-Disposition attachment; client receives the blob, creates an object URL, makes a temporary anchor with that URL and the filename, clicks it programmatically, then revokes the URL.

That covers the whole round trip clearly. One to sit with while it finishes, you mentioned the route gets wired to the controller, but not what stops a non admin user from hitting that export endpoint directly. Don't answer now, just turn it over.

Here's the score: you named all 5 files that were actually planned, no misses there. But the agent also touched a sixth file on its own, server/middleware/requireAdmin.js, which wasn't in anyone's plan. I won't say yet what it does. Given the question I left you with a moment ago, what do you reckon its job is?

Guessing it's new middleware that checks the authenticated user's role is admin before letting requireAuth-passed requests reach the export route, probably added because the existing requireAuth only checked login, not admin privilege.

That matches what the diff shows, requireAdmin runs before the controller and calls next() only when the user is an admin. Three things you didn't mention: the admin.js helper reads the response as a blob rather than JSON, which is the one place this call differs from every other fetch in the app; the download only happens because the controller sets Content-Disposition, without it the CSV text would just open in the tab; and the controller never writes SQL itself, it calls `allForExport()` in server/db/orders.js, which is where you'd go to change which columns get exported.

Now server/middleware/requireAdmin.js, the one that was not in the plan. Before I explain what it added - is the difference between authentication and authorisation clear to you?
Yes, authentication checks who you are, authorisation checks what you're allowed to do, requireAuth handles the former and requireAdmin the latter.

Right, so this is exactly the gap. The file checks that split directly:

```
if (req.user?.role !== 'admin') return res.status(403).json({ error: 'Forbidden' });
```

That line runs after requireAuth has already confirmed there's a logged in user, it's asking a second, separate question, is this particular user an admin, and refusing with 403 if not. Without it, any signed-in account, not just admins, could hit the export route and pull every order in the table.

This file wasn't part of what you asked for, the agent added it on its own. Keeping it or ripping it out is your call, not mine, and I'm not touching the code either way.

Last one. Your teammate says the CSV should not include customer emails. Which file do you edit to drop that column?
server/db/orders.js, in the allForExport() query/column list.

Not quite, hold that thought against what I told you a moment ago. The controller doesn't just forward whatever allForExport() returns, it hands toCsv a separate COLUMNS list. If the query still selects the email column but COLUMNS doesn't mention it, does the CSV show an email column or not?

Let admins download the orders table as CSV
